title: While It Was Happening
overview: Tell about an ordinary day that did not go to plan. Say what you did for a long time, and how things were: I worked there for two years. Say what was already going on when something happened: I was waiting when the call came. Join it all up with when, while, then, after that and eventually.
learningPath: The lesson: listen once, then listen again with the page open.
Words: 28 words in four groups. Listen, say, check.
Patterns: 3 cards. Read the worked example before the practice.
Reading: a short account, an information text and a notice.
Speaking: tap the mic. Say it. Listen back. Use the checklist.
Writing: 4 tasks. Compare each one with the model.
Practice: 6 sets. Mark them with the key and count.
lectureScript:
Hello. This is Unit 5.
In this unit you tell about a day that did not go to plan.
You say what happened, and what was going on around it.
First, the past for a long time.
Some things in the past lasted a long time.
A job. A flat. A feeling.
For those, use the plain past.
I worked there for two years.
I lived near the market.
I was happy in that job.
The time is over, so the verb is in the past.
And you can say how long, with for.
Listen.
I worked in a shop for two years.
She had that phone for a long time.
We were neighbours for three years.
Now, the background.
Sometimes one thing was already going on.
Then something else happened.
For the thing that was already going on, use was or were, plus -ing.
I was waiting.
The rain was falling.
They were talking.
Now put the two together.
I was waiting when the call came.
Listen again.
The long thing: I was waiting.
The short thing: the call came.
The short thing cuts into the long one.
Say it with when.
I was crossing the road when I noticed the sign.
Now say it with while.
While I was crossing the road, I noticed the sign.
When goes in front of the short thing.
While goes in front of the long thing.
Both lines mean the same.
Careful here.
After was and were, the verb needs -ing.
Not: I was wait. Yes: I was waiting.
And the short event keeps the plain past.
Not: the call was coming. Yes: the call came.
Now, carrying the account forward.
An account is more than one line.
So you need words to join the lines.
Then.
After that.
Afterwards.
Eventually.
Listen.
I left at eight. Then I saw the roadworks.
After that, I took a detour.
Eventually, I arrived at ten.
Put a comma after After that at the start of a line.
Then needs no comma. Then I walked.
One more small word: during.
During comes before a naming word.
During the roadworks. During the morning.
While comes before a whole sentence.
While I was waiting.
Now the words.
Twenty-eight words, in four groups.
Things that happen to you: occur, spill, crash, jam, notice, realise, panic, manage.
On the way: detour, traffic, passenger, route, roadworks, pavement, crossing, fare.
Telling what happened: unexpectedly, while, during, afterwards, eventually, immediately.
How it felt: anxious, surprised, annoyed, relieved, calm, upset.
One last thing.
Say how you felt. It makes the account real.
I was anxious. Then I was relieved.
Nothing here is serious.
A spilled cup. A jammed printer. A late bus.
Now go to the words.
Listen, say each one, and check.

outcomes.outcome: Talk about a job, a home or a feeling that lasted, using the plain past and for.
outcomes.evidence: Pattern 1 practice self-checked; Practice 1 eight or more of ten; Speaking 1 recording; Writing 1 against the model; Quiz item 1.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can say what I did for a long time in the past.

outcomes.outcome: Use was and were with -ing to say what was already going on when something else happened.
outcomes.evidence: Pattern 2 practice self-checked; Practice 2 six or more of eight; Writing 2 against the model; Quiz items 2 and 11.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can write what was going on when something happened.

outcomes.outcome: Join two past actions with when, while and during, and keep the two verb forms apart.
outcomes.evidence: Pattern 2 and Pattern 3 practice self-checked; Practice 3 six or more of eight; Speaking 2 and Speaking 4 recordings; Quiz items 3, 4 and 10.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can join two past actions with when and while.

outcomes.outcome: Write a short account of four to six lines, joined with then, after that, afterwards and eventually.
outcomes.evidence: Pattern 3 practice self-checked; Practice 4 all six in order; Writing 3 and Writing 4 against the models and their criteria; Quiz item 8.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can write a short account with the lines joined in order.

outcomes.outcome: Read a short account or a notice and work out a new word from the words around it.
outcomes.evidence: Comprehension items 3, 6 and 8; Practice 5 fourteen or more of sixteen; Practice 6 five or more of six; Quiz items 5, 6, 7, 9 and 12.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can guess what a new word means from the rest of the text.

outcomes.outcome: Follow a short spoken account of a journey and pick out a detail you did not catch at first.
outcomes.evidence: The lesson, played twice; the three readings played with the Listen button and answered with the page covered; Speaking 5 played back.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can follow a short spoken account of a journey and pick out the details.

outcomes.outcome: Say the three -ed endings and this unit's long words clearly enough to be understood.
outcomes.evidence: Speaking 3 recording, played back against the three -ed groups and the five long words.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can say the -ed endings and the long words clearly.

outcomes.outcome: Ask what happened, answer the same questions, and keep a short exchange going.
outcomes.evidence: Speaking 5 recording, five questions and five answers; Speaking 6 one-minute recording; the assignment recording.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can ask what happened and answer when someone asks me.

words.meaning: Happen. It is used more on notices and in writing than in talk.
words.example: The problem occurred at about nine o'clock.
practice: Short delays occur every day on this route.
What time did the fault occur?
It occurred while I was waiting at the crossing.
Occur, occurred: the r is written twice.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for two notices that use occur. Say each one again with happen, and tell it which one sounds more like talk.

words.meaning: Let a drink or a powder fall out of its cup, bottle or bag.
words.example: I spilled my coffee on the table.
practice: Be careful. The bottle is full and it will spill.
She spilled some water, then she cleaned it up.
I was carrying two mugs when I spilled one.
Spill, spilled: just add -ed.
words.tutor: Tell the tutor about a small spill: what it was, and what you did next. Ask it to check that spilled has -ed.

words.meaning: Stop working all at once, like a computer. It is also the loud sound a thing makes when it falls.
words.example: My computer crashed and I lost the page.
practice: The phone crashed while I was writing a message.
A box of tins fell off the shelf with a crash.
Save your work. This old machine crashes every week.
Crash, crashed: just add -ed.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for three sentences with crash about machines, and three about a loud sound. Say which group each one is in.

words.meaning: A lot of cars and buses that cannot move. A machine can jam too, when paper is stuck inside it.
words.example: We sat in a traffic jam for forty minutes.
practice: The printer jammed, so nothing came out.
There is a jam on the main road this morning.
The paper jammed while I was printing the form.
Jam, jammed: the m is written twice.
words.starter: We sat in a jam for
words.tutor: Ask the tutor to give you two lines with jam: one about a road and one about a printer. Then say a third one of your own.

words.meaning: See or hear something without looking for it.
words.example: I noticed a new sign on the door.
practice: Did you notice the roadworks on your way here?
I did not notice the time. I was reading.
She noticed that the shop was closed.
Notice, noticed: it ends in e, so add only d.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor the difference between look at and notice. Then give it one sentence of your own for each.

words.meaning: Understand something that was already true before you understood it.
words.example: I realised that I was on the wrong bus.
practice: Halfway there, I realised I had no ticket.
When did you realise the road was closed?
She realised her mistake and went back.
Realise, realised: it ends in e, so add only d.
words.tutor: Tell the tutor one thing you realised too late on a journey. Ask it whether realised is the right word there, or noticed.

words.meaning: Feel very worried for a short time and stop thinking clearly.
words.example: I panicked for a moment, then I read the sign.
practice: Do not panic. There is another bus in ten minutes.
He panicked, then he sat down and made a plan.
There was no panic. Everybody waited quietly.
Panic, panicked: a k is added before the -ed.
words.starter: I panicked for a moment, then
words.tutor: Ask the tutor why panicked has a k in it and liked does not. Then say three more verbs that end in -ic.

words.meaning: Do something that was not easy.
words.example: I managed to get to work by ten.
practice: We managed to find another route.
Did you manage to print the form?
She managed it without any help.
Manage, managed: it ends in e, so add only d.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for five sentences with managed to. Say which of them could be about your own week.

words.meaning: A longer way round, because the usual way is closed.
words.example: The bus took a detour around the roadworks.
practice: A detour adds ten minutes to the journey.
We made a detour past the market.
The sign showed the detour in red.
There was a detour, because a bridge was closed.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor to describe a detour in three lines: why, where and how much longer. Then describe one of your own.

words.meaning: All the cars and buses moving on a road.
words.example: The traffic was very slow this morning.
practice: There is a lot of traffic at eight o'clock.
We left early to avoid the traffic.
The traffic stopped at the crossing.
Traffic is a word you cannot count. Never say traffics.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor why we say a lot of traffic and not many traffics. Then give it two more words that work the same way.

words.meaning: A person who travels in a bus, a train, a taxi or a car, and does not drive.
words.example: The passengers waited on the pavement.
practice: Every passenger must have a ticket.
I was a passenger, not the driver.
The bus was full, so ten passengers waited for the next one.
Passenger has three parts: pas-sen-ger.
words.tutor: Say the word passenger to the tutor three times. Ask it which part is the loud one.

words.meaning: The way a bus, a train or a person goes from one place to another.
words.example: Bus route 9 goes past the hospital.
practice: The driver knew a faster route.
Which route did you take this morning?
The route changed during the roadworks.
Route sounds like root.
words.tutor: Describe your route to the shops in three lines. Ask the tutor to say it back and name every place you mentioned.

words.meaning: Work on a road, so that part of it is closed.
words.example: There are roadworks on the main road.
practice: The roadworks started last month.
Because of the roadworks, the bus was late.
Roadworks is two words joined: road and works.
The sign said: roadworks for two weeks.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for three other words made of two words joined, like roadworks. Then say what each half means.

words.meaning: The path at the side of a road, for people walking.
words.example: Walk on the pavement, not on the road.
practice: The pavement was wet after the rain.
She waited on the pavement with her bag.
The pavement was closed for two days.
Pavement has three parts: pave-ment.
words.starter: I was standing on the pavement when
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for two safety lines that use the word pavement. Read each one out loud and copy the sound of it.

words.meaning: The place where people can walk over a road.
words.example: Wait at the crossing until the light changes.
practice: There is a crossing outside the school.
I was standing at the crossing when the bus passed.
Use the crossing. It is safer.
Crossing comes from cross, plus -ing.
words.starter: I waited at the crossing and
words.tutor: Ask the tutor to give you directions that use crossing twice. Then say the same directions back in your own words.

words.meaning: The price you pay to travel on a bus, a train or a taxi.
words.example: The fare is 2 for a short journey.
practice: I paid my fare to the driver.
The fare went up in January.
Ask the driver about the fare before you sit down.
Fare and fair sound the same, but they mean different things.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for one sentence with fare and one with fair. Say both out loud and listen for the same sound.

words.meaning: In a way nobody planned.
words.example: The road closed unexpectedly on Monday.
practice: My phone unexpectedly stopped working.
She arrived unexpectedly early.
Unexpectedly, the bus came on time.
Say it in parts: un-ex-pec-ted-ly.
words.tutor: Say unexpectedly to the tutor five times. Ask it to count the parts it heard and compare that with five.

words.meaning: At the same time as. It comes before a whole sentence.
words.example: While I was waiting, I read the notice.
practice: The rain started while we were on the bus.
He read his messages while the train was moving.
While she was talking, I wrote it down.
While joins two things that happened at the same time.
words.tutor: Give the tutor two things that happened at the same time. Ask it to join them with while and check where the comma goes.

words.meaning: Inside a time that you have already named. A naming word comes after it.
words.example: The lights went off during the storm.
practice: There were no buses during the roadworks.
I did not speak during the call.
During the morning, the traffic was very slow.
After during comes a naming word, never a whole sentence.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for four lines with during. Then change each one to a line with while, and see what has to change.

words.meaning: Later, once the first thing has finished.
words.example: We waited for an hour. Afterwards, we walked.
practice: The meeting finished at four, and afterwards I went home.
Afterwards, I realised my mistake.
First the detour, and afterwards the traffic.
Afterwards ends in s. Say: af-ter-wards.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor to tell a two-line story that uses afterwards. Then tell it one of your own about a journey.

words.meaning: In the end, after a long time.
words.example: Eventually, the bus arrived.
practice: We waited and waited. Eventually, the road opened.
Eventually, I managed to print the form.
The printer jammed four times, but eventually it worked.
Eventually has five parts: e-ven-tu-al-ly.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for the difference between eventually and immediately. Then use each one in a line about waiting for a bus.

words.meaning: At once, with no wait at all.
words.example: I noticed the sign immediately.
practice: Call the office immediately if the machine stops.
She answered immediately.
Immediately after the crossing, turn left.
Immediately has five parts: im-me-di-ate-ly.
words.tutor: Say immediately and eventually to the tutor. Ask it which one you said more clearly, and say that one again.

words.meaning: Worried about something that might happen.
words.example: I felt anxious about being late.
practice: She was anxious, so she left an hour early.
There is no need to feel anxious. You have plenty of time.
I was anxious during the wait, but it was fine.
Anxious has two parts: anx-ious.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for the difference between anxious and afraid. Use anxious in one line about a bus and one about a form.

words.meaning: Feeling that something has happened that you did not expect.
words.example: I was surprised to see the road closed.
practice: He looked surprised when I told him.
I was surprised by how quiet the street was.
She was surprised, but she was not annoyed.
Surprised ends in -ed, like a past word.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for one thing that would surprise a passenger on a bus. Then say whether it would surprise you.

words.meaning: A little angry, because something is not right.
words.example: I was annoyed about the delay.
practice: The passengers were annoyed, but they waited.
Do not get annoyed with the machine.
She was annoyed when the printer jammed again.
Annoyed has two n letters: an-noyed.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor to put annoyed, angry and upset in order, from small to big. Then say a line for each one.

words.meaning: Happy because a worry has gone.
words.example: I was relieved when the bus finally came.
practice: She was relieved to find her keys.
We were relieved that nobody was late.
First anxious, then relieved.
In relieved, the i comes before the e.
words.tutor: Tell the tutor a two-line story: anxious first, relieved after. Ask it whether the second line really answers the first.

words.meaning: Quiet inside, and not worried.
words.example: Stay calm and read the notice.
practice: He was calm, even during the long delay.
The street was calm after the traffic went.
Sit down and stay calm.
In calm, the l is quiet. Say: cahm.
words.tutor: Say calm to the tutor and ask whether it heard an l sound. There should be none.

words.meaning: Unhappy, because something has gone wrong.
words.example: She was upset about the spilled coffee.
practice: Do not be upset. It was only a cup of water.
He was upset, so I made him a tea.
I was more annoyed than upset.
Upset has two parts: up-set.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for three small things that could upset somebody on a journey. Say which one would upset you least.

grammar.title: I worked there for two years: a habit and a state
grammar.explanation:
Some things in the past went on for a long time.
A job. A home. A feeling. Something you did every day.
For all of those, use the plain past.
The time is over now, so the verb is in the past.
Say how long with for: for two years, for six months.
grammar.rule:
A job or a home:
I worked there for two years.
She lived near the market for six months.

A state, with was or were:
I was happy in that job.
We were neighbours for three years.

A habit, with every or always:
I walked to work every day.
The bus was always late.

How long: for two years, for six months, for an hour.
When: last year, in January, two years ago.

I, he, she, it: was.
You, we, they: were.
grammar.workedExample:
Task: say that a job lasted. Facts: a shop, two years, finished last year.
1. Who? I.
2. What did I do? work. It is finished, so: worked.
3. Where? in a shop.
4. How long? two years. Put for in front: for two years.
5. In order: I worked in a shop for two years.
6. Add the feeling, with was: I was happy there.
7. Check: is every verb in the past? worked, was. Yes.
grammar.mistake:
It is easy to use the -ing form for a long job.
No: I was working there for two years.
Yes: I worked there for two years.
The -ing form is the background form, and it is on the next card.
A long, finished time takes the plain past.
grammar.tip: A finished job, a finished home, a finished feeling: plain past, and for.
grammar.practice:
Write the past form of the verb in brackets. Then read the line.
1. I ___ in that office for three years. (work)
2. She ___ near the station for six months. (live)
3. We ___ neighbours for a long time. (be)
4. He ___ to work every day. (walk)
5. The traffic ___ always slow in the morning. (be)
6. They ___ that old car for ten years. (have)
7. I ___ the same route every day. (take)
grammar.answers:
1. worked  2. lived  3. were  4. walked  5. was  6. had  7. took
Wrong on 3? We takes were, not was.
Wrong on 5? The traffic is one thing, so it takes was.
Wrong on 6 or 7? Have and take do not add -ed. They change: had, took.
Six or seven right: go on. Fewer? Read the rule again and mark it once more.

grammar.title: I was waiting when the call came: the background
grammar.explanation:
One thing was already going on. Then something else happened.
For the thing that was already going on, use was or were, plus -ing.
For the thing that happened, use the plain past.
Together they make a background and an event.
grammar.rule:
The background: was or were, plus -ing.
I was waiting.
The rain was falling.
They were talking.

The event: the plain past.
The call came.
I noticed the sign.

Join them with when:
I was waiting when the call came.

Or with while, in front of the long one:
While I was waiting, the call came.

when goes in front of the short event.
while goes in front of the long background.
Both lines mean the same thing.

After a while part at the start, write a comma.
grammar.workedExample:
Task: join these two. Long: I cross the road. Short: I notice the sign.
1. Which one lasted longer? Crossing the road.
2. Make it the background: was, plus -ing. I was crossing the road.
3. The other one is the event. Plain past: I noticed the sign.
4. Join with when, in front of the event: I was crossing the road when I noticed the sign.
5. Now try while, in front of the background: While I was crossing the road, I noticed the sign.
6. Check: only one verb has -ing. Yes.
7. Check: is there a comma after the while part? Yes.
grammar.mistake:
It is easy to drop the -ing after was.
No: I was wait when the call came.
Yes: I was waiting when the call came.
And the short event keeps the plain past.
No: I was waiting when the call was coming.
Yes: I was waiting when the call came.
grammar.tip: Long thing: was plus -ing. Short thing: plain past. when points at the short one.
grammar.practice:
Write the right form of the verb in brackets.
1. I ___ (wait) at the crossing when the bus passed.
2. While she ___ (talk) to the driver, I paid the fare.
3. The printer jammed while I ___ (print) the form.
4. We ___ (sit) in a traffic jam when the phone rang.
5. It ___ (rain) while we were walking on the pavement.
6. They were talking when the lights ___ (go) off.
7. Join these two with when: I carry two cups. I spill one.
grammar.answers:
1. was waiting  2. was talking  3. was printing  4. were sitting  5. was raining  6. went
7. I was carrying two cups when I spilled one.
Wrong on 4? We takes were, not was.
Wrong on 6? The lights going off is the short event, so it keeps the plain past: went.
Wrong on 7? Carrying is the long thing, so it takes was plus -ing. Spilled is the short event.
Six or seven right: go on. Fewer? Read the rule again and mark it once more.

grammar.title: Then, and after that: joining one event to the next
grammar.explanation:
An account is more than one line.
Join the lines, so the reader knows the order.
Use then, after that, afterwards, eventually and immediately.
Each one points forward to the next thing.
grammar.rule:
In order:
I left at eight.
Then I saw the roadworks.
After that, I took a detour.
Eventually, I arrived at ten.

then: the very next thing. No comma is needed.
after that: the next thing, with a comma at the start of a line.
afterwards: later, once the first thing has finished.
eventually: in the end, after a long wait.
immediately: at once, with no wait at all.

You can also open a line with a time part:
During the roadworks, the bus was slow.
While I was waiting, I read the notice.

during comes before a naming word.
while comes before a whole sentence.
grammar.workedExample:
Task: join these four steps into an account.
Steps: leave at eight, see the roadworks, take a detour, arrive at ten.
1. Step one needs no joining word: I left at eight.
2. Step two is the very next thing: Then I saw the roadworks.
3. Step three follows it: After that, I took a detour. Note the comma.
4. Step four came a long time later: Eventually, I arrived at ten.
5. Read the four lines out loud. Does the order match the day? Yes.
6. Check: every verb in the past. left, saw, took, arrived. Yes.
grammar.mistake:
It is easy to start every line with then.
No: Then I left. Then I saw it. Then I walked. Then I arrived.
Yes: I left at eight. Then I saw it. After that, I walked. Eventually, I arrived.
Spread the joining words out, and the reader can follow you.
grammar.tip: Four steps, four different signposts: nothing, then, after that, eventually.
grammar.practice:
Write then, after that, afterwards, eventually or immediately. Use each one once.
1. The printer jammed. ___ I opened it and took the paper out.
2. We waited at the stop for forty minutes. ___, a bus came.
3. Do not wait. If the machine stops, call the office ___.
4. The meeting finished at four, and ___ I walked home.
5. Step three of four: ___, I took a detour past the market.
6. Put these in order: a. Then I noticed the sign. b. Eventually, I found the right stop. c. I left the house at eight.
grammar.answers:
1. Then  2. Eventually  3. immediately  4. afterwards  5. After that  6. c, a, b
Wrong on 2? Forty minutes is a long wait, so eventually fits.
Wrong on 3? Immediately means at once. Then would put it after something else.
Wrong on 4? Afterwards means later, once the meeting has finished.
Wrong on 6? The line with no joining word opens the account.
Five or six right: go on. Fewer? Read the rule again and mark it once more.

readings.title: The Morning the Road Closed
readings.setting: A walk to the bus stop and a slow ride to work, on a Monday morning.
readings.passage:
On Monday I left the house at eight, the same as every week.
I worked in that office for three years, so I knew the route well.
I was walking to the stop when I noticed a new sign on the pavement.
It said: ROADWORKS. BUS 9 IS ON A DETOUR.
For a moment I panicked, because I had a meeting at nine.
Then I read the sign again. It was short and clear.
The stop was fifty metres away, on the other side of the crossing.
I waited there with about ten other passengers.
While we were waiting, one of them spilled her coffee on her bag.
She was annoyed at first, but she laughed about it afterwards.
Eventually the bus came. The traffic was slow, and we sat in a jam for ten minutes.
I paid my fare and looked out of the window at the closed road.
I arrived at five past nine. I was surprised, and I was very relieved.
Nobody minded that I was late. Two other people were late as well.

readings.title: Why a Bus Takes a Detour
readings.setting: A short help page from a bus company, about roadworks and changed stops.
readings.passage:
A detour is a longer way round. A bus takes one when the usual route is closed.
Roadworks are the most common reason. A road may be closed for a day, or for a month.
Sometimes a road closes unexpectedly, and the notice goes up the same morning.
The bus company puts a notice at every stop on the route.
The notice says which stops have moved, and how far.
It also says how much longer the journey will take.
During a detour, a bus is often five or ten minutes late.
The fare does not change. You pay the same price for the longer journey.
Passengers sometimes feel anxious, because the bus goes down a street they do not know.
The driver knows the detour and will call out the stops.
If you are not sure, ask the driver before you sit down.
Roadworks can also close a pavement. Then a crossing may move a few metres.
Look for the small signs on the pavement. They show the new way.
A detour ends when the work finishes, and the old route comes back.

readings.title: Notice at Stop 14
readings.setting: A printed notice inside the shelter at a bus stop on the main road.
readings.passage:
BUS STOP 14: PLEASE READ

ROADWORKS ON THE MAIN ROAD
From Monday 6 to Friday 24.

Bus 9 and Bus 12 are on a detour.
This stop has moved. The new stop is 50 metres along the pavement, past the crossing.

What this means for you
Buses are about 10 minutes later than usual.
The fare is the same. Pay the driver as usual.
The crossing outside the chemist is closed. Use the crossing outside the post office.

If your bus does not come
Wait 15 minutes. Then press the help button on the post beside this notice.
Do not walk in the road. Stay on the pavement.

We are sorry for the delay. Thank you for waiting.

comprehension.q: What did the new sign on the pavement say?
comprehension.a: Roadworks, and Bus 9 is on a detour.
comprehension.why: Line 4 gives the sign word for word: ROADWORKS. BUS 9 IS ON A DETOUR.

comprehension.q: How long did the writer work in that office?
comprehension.why: Line 2: I worked in that office for three years. The plain past and for show a finished length of time.

comprehension.q: One passenger spilled her coffee. What does spilled mean here?
comprehension.a: The coffee came out of her cup and went on her bag.
comprehension.why: The next words are on her bag, so the coffee left the cup and landed somewhere it should not.

comprehension.q: The writer panicked, then read the sign again and stopped worrying. Why?
comprehension.a: The sign showed that the new stop was only fifty metres away.
comprehension.why: The line after the sign gives the distance, so the meeting at nine was still possible.

comprehension.q: Does the fare change while a bus is on a detour?
comprehension.a: No. You pay the same price for the longer journey.
comprehension.why: The text says the fare does not change, and gives the reason in the next line.

comprehension.q: The text says a road can close unexpectedly. What does unexpectedly mean?
comprehension.a: With no warning, in a way nobody planned.
comprehension.why: The same line says the notice goes up the same morning, so there was no time to plan for it.

comprehension.q: You are on a detour and you do not know the street. What does the text tell you to do?
comprehension.a: Ask the driver before you sit down. The driver knows the detour and calls out the stops.
comprehension.why: The last two lines of that part answer exactly this worry, and name the driver as the person who knows.

comprehension.q: Your bus has not come after fifteen minutes. What does the notice tell you to do?
comprehension.a: Press the help button on the post beside the notice.
comprehension.why: That is the only instruction under the heading If your bus does not come.

comprehension.q: The crossing outside the chemist is closed. Which crossing should you use?
comprehension.a: The crossing outside the post office.
comprehension.why: The notice names the closed crossing and the open one in the same line.

comprehension.q: How far along the pavement is the new stop, and what do you pass?
comprehension.a: Fifty metres along the pavement, past the crossing.
comprehension.why: The notice gives the distance and the crossing in one line, under the detour heading.

speaking.title: Speaking 1 — I worked there for two years
speaking.instructions:
Listen. Say each line.
I worked in a shop for two years.
She lived near the market for six months.
We were neighbours for three years.
I walked to work every day.
The bus was always late.
Now say three lines of your own.
A made-up job, class or flat is fine.
Tap the mic. Say your three lines.
Tap the mic again. Listen.
Check: is every verb in the past?
Check: did you say how long, with for?
speaking.tutor: Tell the tutor about a job or a flat that lasted two years. Ask it to repeat back only the past verbs it heard.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — I was waiting when the call came
speaking.instructions:
Listen. Say each line.
I was waiting when the call came.
While I was waiting, the call came.
I was crossing the road when I noticed the sign.
While she was talking to the driver, I paid the fare.
We were sitting in a jam when the phone rang.
Tap the mic. Say the five lines.
Tap the mic again. Listen.
Check: does only one verb in each line have -ing?
Check: after a while part at the start, did you pause for the comma?
speaking.tutor: Give the tutor one long action and one short one. Ask it to join them with when, then with while, and compare both lines with yours.

speaking.title: Speaking 3 — The -ed ending, and the long words
speaking.instructions:
The -ed ending has three sounds. Listen and repeat.
After t or d, -ed is a whole new part: wait-ed, start-ed.
After k, p, s or ch, -ed sounds like t: worked, stopped, crossed, noticed, panicked.
After most other sounds, -ed sounds like d: realised, managed, spilled, jammed, arrived.
Now the long words. Say them in parts.
un-ex-pec-ted-ly
im-me-di-ate-ly
e-ven-tu-al-ly
pas-sen-ger
road-works
Tap the mic. Say the three -ed groups and the five long words.
Tap the mic again. Listen.
Check: does waited have one part more than worked? It should.
Check: can you hear five parts in unexpectedly?
speaking.tutor: Say the five long words to the tutor in any order. Ask it which ones it heard, and check them against your list.

speaking.title: Speaking 4 — Tell the morning in order
speaking.instructions:
Here is a morning in four steps. Listen.
I left the house at eight.
Then I saw the roadworks on the main road.
After that, I took a detour past the market.
Eventually, I arrived at ten past nine.
Now change the four steps to your own. A made-up morning is fine.
Use a different signpost each time: nothing, then, after that, eventually.
Tap the mic. Say your four lines.
Tap the mic again. Listen.
Check: four steps, four different signposts?
Check: is the order the same as the morning?
speaking.tutor: Say your four steps to the tutor. Ask it to tell you back only the signpost words, in order, and see if they match.

speaking.title: Speaking 5 — Ask and answer: what happened?
speaking.instructions:
Five questions. Listen, then say each one.
What happened?
When did it happen?
Where were you?
What were you doing at the time?
How did you feel afterwards?
Now the answers. Listen, then say each one.
I missed my bus.
It happened on Monday morning.
I was at the stop outside the chemist.
I was reading a notice about the roadworks.
I was annoyed at first, then relieved.
Tap the mic. Ask the five questions, then answer them yourself.
Tap the mic again. Listen.
Check: does every answer match its question?
Check: did the fourth answer use was or were, plus -ing?
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor to put the five questions to you, one at a time. Answer each one, then ask it the same five back.

speaking.title: Speaking 6 — One minute: the day it did not go to plan
speaking.instructions:
Talk for about one minute. A made-up day is fine.
Plan it first. Say these four things, in this order.
One: where you were and what you were doing.
Two: what happened unexpectedly.
Three: what you did about it.
Four: how you felt at the end.
Here is a short model. Listen.
On Tuesday I was walking to the station.
While I was crossing the road, I noticed a sign about roadworks.
I panicked for a moment. Then I took a detour past the park.
Eventually I got there, and I was very relieved.
Tap the mic. Talk for one minute.
Tap the mic again. Listen.
Check: at least one line with was or were, plus -ing?
Check: at least two signposts, such as then, after that or eventually?
Check: one feeling word at the end?
speaking.tutor: Tell the tutor your one minute. Ask it to name every feeling word it heard, and to say where one more would fit.

writing.title: Writing 1 — Something that lasted
writing.prompt:
Write four sentences about a job, a home or a course that lasted a long time and has now finished.
You can make it up.
Use the plain past, and say how long with for.
writing.model:
I worked in a small shop for two years.
I lived near the market for those same two years.
I walked to work every day, and I was happy there.
The shop closed last year, and I was upset about it.
writing.criteria:
Four sentences.
Every verb in the past.
At least two sentences say how long, with for.
One sentence says how you felt, with was.
writing.support:
First write four short notes: what, where, how long, how you felt.
Like this: shop, near the market, two years, happy.
Then turn each note into one sentence.
writing.extension: Add a fifth sentence that starts with Eventually.

writing.title: Writing 2 — What was going on
writing.prompt:
Write three pairs of past actions.
In each pair, one thing lasted and one thing happened.
Join each pair with when. Then write one of the pairs again with while.
writing.model:
I was waiting at the crossing when the bus passed.
I was printing the form when the printer jammed.
We were sitting in the traffic when the phone rang.
While we were sitting in the traffic, the phone rang.
writing.criteria:
Three sentences joined with when, and one more with while.
Every long action has was or were, plus -ing.
Every short action is in the plain past.
A comma after the while part at the start of the last sentence.
writing.support:
Take one pair only.
Write the long action first: I was waiting.
Write the short one next: the bus passed.
Now put when between them, and do the other two pairs the same way.
writing.extension: Add one more pair. Make the long action something you were carrying, and the short one a spill.

writing.title: Writing 3 — A morning that did not go to plan
writing.prompt:
Write six lines about a morning that did not go to plan.
A made-up morning is fine.
Tell it in the order it happened, and join the lines with then, after that, afterwards and eventually.
writing.model:
On Monday I left the house at eight.
I was walking to the stop when I noticed a notice about roadworks.
I panicked for a moment, because I had a meeting at nine.
Then I read the notice again and found the new stop.
After that, I waited with about ten other passengers.
Eventually the bus came, and I arrived only five minutes late.
writing.criteria:
Six lines, in the order it happened.
Every verb in the past.
At least three different joining words.
At least one line with was or were, plus -ing.
One feeling word from this unit.
writing.support:
First list the six steps in single words, in order.
Like this: left, walked, saw, panicked, waited, arrived.
Then write one line for each word, and add the joining words last.
writing.extension: Rewrite the last line so that it starts with a feeling: I was relieved, because the bus came.

writing.title: Writing 4 — A short message about the detour
writing.prompt:
Write a message of four lines to somebody who takes the same bus as you.
You can make the person up.
Tell them what has changed and what to do. Take the facts from the Notice at Stop 14.
writing.model:
The main road is closed for roadworks until Friday 24.
Bus 9 is on a detour, so it is about ten minutes later than usual.
Our stop has moved 50 metres along the pavement, past the crossing.
The fare is the same, and you still pay the driver.
writing.criteria:
Four sentences.
Three facts taken from the notice.
One sentence that says what to do.
Every sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with a full stop.
writing.support:
Read the notice again and mark three facts with your finger.
Write each fact as a short note first.
Then turn each note into one full sentence.
writing.extension: Add a fifth line that says how long the detour lasts.

activities.title: Practice 1 — A long, finished time
activities.instructions:
Write the past form of the verb in brackets.
1. She ___ in that office for four years. (work)
2. We ___ near the station for six months. (live)
3. They ___ neighbours for a long time. (be)
4. He ___ the same route every morning. (take)
5. I ___ that old phone for three years. (have)
6. The traffic ___ always slow at eight. (be)
7. You ___ to work every day last winter. (walk)
8. My sister ___ the fare in cash. (pay)
9. The shop ___ at six every evening. (close)
10. I ___ that notice every morning for a week. (read)
activities.answers:
1. worked  2. lived  3. were  4. took  5. had  6. was  7. walked  8. paid  9. closed  10. read
Wrong on 3 or 6? They takes were. The traffic is one thing, so it takes was.
Wrong on 4, 5, 8 or 10? Take, have, pay and read do not add -ed. They change: took, had, paid, read.
Eight or more of ten: go on. Fewer? Read Pattern 1 again and mark it once more.
activities.solo: Write your answers on paper first. Then mark them with the key and count them. Read the ten lines out loud.

activities.title: Practice 2 — Long thing or short thing?
activities.instructions:
Choose the right form. Write a or b.
1. I (a) waited (b) was waiting at the crossing when the bus passed.
2. While she (a) talked (b) was talking to the driver, I paid the fare.
3. The printer jammed while I (a) printed (b) was printing the form.
4. We were sitting in a jam when the phone (a) rang (b) was ringing.
5. It (a) rained (b) was raining while we were walking on the pavement.
6. They were talking when the lights (a) went (b) were going off.
7. I (a) spilled (b) was spilling my coffee while I was carrying it.
8. He was reading a notice when he (a) realised (b) was realising the time.
activities.answers:
1. b  2. b  3. b  4. a  5. b  6. a  7. a  8. a
The long thing takes was or were, plus -ing. The short event keeps the plain past.
Wrong on 4 or 6? A phone ringing and lights going off are short events.
Wrong on 7 or 8? A spill and a moment of understanding are short events too.
Six or more of eight: go on. Fewer? Read Pattern 2 again.
activities.solo: Cover the answers. Write a or b for all eight. Then mark them and read each full sentence out loud.

activities.title: Practice 3 — when, while or during
activities.instructions:
Write when, while or during.
1. ___ I was waiting, I read the notice.
2. There were no buses ___ the roadworks.
3. I was crossing the road ___ I noticed the sign.
4. ___ the morning, the traffic was very slow.
5. The lights went off ___ we were sitting in the jam.
6. She spilled her coffee ___ she was getting on the bus.
7. I did not speak ___ the call.
8. We were talking ___ the driver called out the stop.
activities.answers:
1. While  2. during  3. when  4. During  5. while  6. while  7. during  8. when
During comes before a naming word: during the call, during the morning.
When and while come before a whole sentence.
When points at the short event. While points at the long one.
Wrong on 3 or 8? Noticing a sign and calling out a stop are short events, so when fits.
Six or more of eight: go on. Fewer? Read Pattern 2 and Pattern 3 again.
activities.solo: Write the eight words on paper and mark them with the key. Copy out the whole line for any you got wrong.

activities.title: Practice 4 — Put the morning in order
activities.instructions:
Put the six lines in order. Write the letters.
a. After that, I waited at the new stop with ten other passengers.
b. On Tuesday I left the house at eight.
c. Eventually the bus came, and the traffic was slow all the way.
d. I was walking to the stop when I noticed a notice about roadworks.
e. I arrived at ten past nine, and I was very relieved.
f. Then I read the notice again and found the new stop.
activities.answers:
b, d, f, a, c, e
Look at the joining word at the start of each line.
On Tuesday opens the morning, and the line with no joining word comes next.
Then follows the notice. After that follows the new stop.
Eventually points to the end of a long wait, and arrived is the last thing that happened.
All six right: go on. Not all? Read Pattern 3 again and do it once more.
activities.solo: Write the six letters on paper. Then read the six lines out loud in your order and check them with the key.

activities.title: Practice 5 — Sort the words
activities.instructions:
Write each word under one of the four headings.
Headings: Things that happen to you. On the way. Telling what happened. How it felt.
Words: detour, anxious, occur, afterwards, fare, manage, relieved, roadworks, immediately, spill, upset, passenger, eventually, notice, crossing, calm.
activities.answers:
Things that happen to you: occur, manage, spill, notice
On the way: detour, fare, roadworks, passenger, crossing
Telling what happened: afterwards, immediately, eventually
How it felt: anxious, relieved, upset, calm
Careful with notice: here it is the verb, meaning see something without looking for it.
Fourteen or more of sixteen: go on. Fewer? Go back to the word list and listen to each one again.
activities.solo: Write the four headings on paper and put each word under one. Then check with the key and say each word out loud.

activities.title: Practice 6 — How did it feel?
activities.instructions:
Choose anxious, surprised, annoyed, relieved, calm or upset. Use each word once.
1. She lost her keys and looked for an hour. Then she found them. She was ___.
2. The bus was twenty minutes late again, for the third day. He was ___.
3. She had a meeting at nine, and the road was closed. She felt ___.
4. He did not expect to see me there at all. He looked ___.
5. Everybody else was worried, but the driver stayed ___ and made a plan.
6. He spilled water on the form, and it was no good any more. He was ___.
activities.answers:
1. relieved  2. annoyed  3. anxious  4. surprised  5. calm  6. upset
Relieved is the feeling after a worry ends. Anxious is the worry before it.
Annoyed is a little angry. Upset is unhappy.
Surprised is for something you did not expect. Calm is quiet inside.
Five or six right: go on. Fewer? Read the How it felt group again.
activities.solo: Write the six words on paper, one for each line. Then mark them with the key and read each full sentence out loud.

quizzes.q: I ___ in that shop for two years, and then I moved.
quizzes.why: A long, finished time takes the plain past: worked. Was working is the background form, for something going on when another thing happened. Work and am working are about now.

quizzes.q: I ___ at the crossing when the bus passed.
quizzes.why: Waiting is the long thing going on, so it takes was plus -ing. Waited would make it a second short event, and the line already has one: the bus passed. Wait and am waiting are about now.

quizzes.q: Which line puts while in the right place?
options: While the call came, I was waiting.
I was waiting while the call.
While I was waiting, the call came.
While I waiting, the call came.
quizzes.a: While I was waiting, the call came.
quizzes.why: While goes in front of the long background: I was waiting. The first line puts while in front of the short event and turns the meaning round. The second stops before its verb. The fourth drops was.

quizzes.q: The printer jammed ___ I was printing the form.
quizzes.why: While joins two things at the same moment, and a whole sentence follows it. During is followed by a naming word: during the morning. Then and afterwards point forward to the next thing, not to the same moment.

options: In the end, after a long time.
At the same time as something else.
quizzes.a: In the end, after a long time.
quizzes.why: Eventually means in the end. At once is immediately. At the same time is while. The last one is first.

quizzes.q: You are standing on the ___ , not in the road.
quizzes.why: The pavement is the path at the side of a road. A crossing is where you walk over a road. A route is the way a bus goes, and a detour is a longer way round.

options: I was realising that I was late.
Realise I was on the wrong bus.
Halfway there, I realised I was on the wrong bus.
quizzes.a: Halfway there, I realised I was on the wrong bus.
quizzes.why: Realise names a moment of understanding, so here it takes the plain past: realised. The first has no past ending. The second uses -ing, which does not fit a moment. The third has no subject.

quizzes.q: Put these in order: a. Eventually, the bus came. b. I left the house at eight. c. Then I saw the roadworks.
quizzes.why: Leaving the house has no joining word, so it opens the account. Then comes next, and eventually points to the end of a long wait. The other orders put the end or the middle first.

quizzes.q: She lost her keys and looked for an hour. Then she found them. How did she feel then?
quizzes.why: Relieved means happy because a worry has gone. Anxious is the worry before she found them. Upset is unhappy and annoyed is a little angry, and neither fits the moment a worry ends.

quizzes.q: ___ the roadworks, there were no buses on this street.
quizzes.why: During comes before a naming word: during the roadworks. While needs a whole sentence after it. Then and afterwards point at the next thing, not at a length of time.

quizzes.q: Which pair is right? We ___ in a jam when the phone ___ .
quizzes.why: We takes were, not was. Sitting in the jam is the long background, so it needs -ing. The phone ringing is the short event, so it keeps the plain past: rang.

quizzes.q: Which word means the price you pay to travel on a bus?
quizzes.why: The fare is the price of the journey. A route is the way the bus goes. Traffic is all the cars and buses on the road. A passenger is a person travelling.

teacherNotes.note: Every card shows one item done before its practice, every exercise has a key with a score line, and every speaking task ends with record, listen back and a short checklist. If you are helping, play the recording together and point at the checklist rather than correcting mid-sentence. The AI tutor is a rehearsal partner here, never the only check on any task.

teacherNotes.type: The two errors worth your attention
teacherNotes.note: The first is the -ing that goes missing: I was wait when the call came. Point at was and ask what has to follow it, then let the learner repair the line. The second is the -ing that spreads: I was waiting when the call was coming. Only one half of the sentence is the background; ask which of the two lasted longer, and the answer decides the forms. Practice 2 puts the two side by side and Practice 3 adds during, which is the other common slip, because it takes a naming word and not a sentence.

teacherNotes.type: Things go wrong, and they stay small
teacherNotes.note: The whole unit turns on an ordinary day that did not go to plan, so spill, crash, jam and panic all appear. They are kept low: a spilled coffee, a jammed printer, a computer that crashes, a bus stop that has moved fifty metres. Nobody is hurt anywhere in the unit, and no task asks the learner to describe a real bad event. Every account task says a made-up day is fine. If a learner chooses to tell something real, follow their lead and never ask for more.

The two source units also taught because and so, Wh- question forms, adjective and noun order, adverbs of manner, imperatives with can and must, word families and exclamation marks. All of those are taught elsewhere in the course and get no card here. Did and didn't, -ed forms, was and were, and the irregular past came, told, felt and thought are Level 1 and are used freely with no card. First, next and finally are Level 1 Unit 15; this unit's third card is then, after that, afterwards, eventually and immediately, which are the ones that carry an account of a past event forward.

No task asks for a real name, a real address, a real journey or any personal detail, and the learner is told throughout that a made-up job, flat, morning or name is fine. Keep that wording. The tutor prompts all rehearse language rather than collect facts, and no task is scored by the tutor alone.

selfAssessment.statement: I can say what I did for a long time in the past.
I can write what was going on when something happened.
I can join two past actions with when and while.
I can write a short account with the lines joined in order.
I can guess what a new word means from the rest of the text.
I can follow a short spoken account of a journey and pick out the details.
I can say the -ed endings and the long words clearly.
I can ask what happened and answer when someone asks me.

assignment.title: The day it did not go to plan
assignment.instructions:
Two parts. A made-up day is fine, and you can use made-up names.
1. Tap the mic. Tell the day in about six lines. Say where you were and what you were doing, what happened unexpectedly, what you did about it, and how you felt at the end. Use at least one line with was or were, plus -ing.
2. Write the same day in six lines, like Writing 3. Join the lines with at least three different signposts: then, after that, afterwards, eventually or immediately.
Listen to your recording once before you send it, and read your six lines out loud.
assignment.submissionType: Audio recording and a written account
